ruling.recommended_action: Refund $1.86 to the rider's original payment method (surge differential where the rider was not given a compliant notice)
ruling.reasoning:
Safety screen: F10–F13 contain no threat, harassment, sexual remark, dangerous-driving or accident allegation; dispute type is fare, so I rule. safety_concern = none.

Fare analysis. The trip was quoted $10.02 at 1× (F6) and billed $11.88 at 1.3× (F5, F7); the surge rose from 1× to 1.3× before trip start (F8). Route deviation is not in issue: actual 2.4 km vs optimal 2.5 km, i.e. −0.1 km (F1, F3) — within the RD-1 1 km tolerance, so no deviation refund.

Surge notice (SURGE-1). The driver must give in-app notice before/at pickup stating (a) the new multiplier, (b) the revised estimated fare, and (c) the option to cancel without penalty. F9 states all three: "Fares are 1.3× higher right now. Your new estimated fare is $12.65. You can cancel for free." It was sent 14:10:20, before the 14:13:00 trip start. The rider's argument that the notice's $12.65 differs from the billed $11.88 does not make the notice non-compliant — SURGE-1 requires the revised estimated fare (an estimate), and the actual fare came out lower; the notice still gave a real opportunity to cancel free. So the rider WAS notified.

Consequence (SURGE-2 row 1: surge rose, rider notified, rider rode → no_action) would normally leave the charge standing. But SURGE-3's differential formula controls the amount where the fare exceeds the quote: (trip multiplier − quote multiplier) × surgeable subtotal = (1.3 − 1) × $8.18 = $2.45 (F8), capped at the $1.86 by which the actual fare exceeds the quote ($11.88 − $10.02 = $1.86, F6/F7/F8). The booking fee $1.25 is not surged (F7) and is excluded; time and distance components are unaffected by the multiplier. Applying the $1.86 cap and refunding it in full is the only reading that keeps the rider from paying any surge uplift he was not properly bound to; the record's own figure for the surplus is $1.86.

Amount: refund_partial $1.86 ($11.88 − $10.02), settled from the fare records (F5–F8) — under $10, so the system decides (TH-1 / TH-2, per C1). Evidence is complete: continuous GPS (F1–F3), timestamped chats (F12), a timestamped surge log (F9), and fare records (F5–F8). Confidence 0.82; profile facts (F14, F15) were not used to decide. No repeat-deviation clause applies (F15 route upheld = 0) and no no-show clause applies, so no flag_account.

element_findings.element: Surge notice states the new multiplier (SURGE-1)
element_findings.reason: Notice text: "Fares are 1.3× higher right now" — the new 1.3× multiplier is stated.

element_findings.element: Surge notice states the revised estimated fare (SURGE-1)
element_findings.reason: "Your new estimated fare is $12.65" gives a revised estimated fare; the requirement is an estimate, and the billed fare ($11.88) came in below it, so the notice was not misleading as to what would be charged.
"You can cancel for free" is an explicit free-cancel statement, not the weaker "cancellation fees may apply".

element_findings.element: Notice given before or at trip start (SURGE-1)
element_findings.reason: Sent in_app at 14:10:20; trip started 14:13:00, so notice preceded the trip.

element_findings.element: Cause of the fare difference over the quote is surge alone (SURGE-3)
element_findings.reason: Distance was 0.1 km under the optimal route (no RD refund), and the $1.86 excess over the quote is attributed to the 1× → 1.3× increase, with (1.3−1) × $8.18 = $2.45 capped at $1.86.

rejected_claims.reason: The rider says the notice was misleading because the quoted fare in it differed from the charge, but the record (F9) states the multiplier, the revised estimated fare and free cancellation before trip start — SURGE-1's notice elements are all present, so non-notification is not established.
There is no compliant basis for a full-surge refund: notice was compliant and the surplus over the quote is $1.86 (F6–F8), which is the amount refunded.
